title: 2D vs 3D CNNs
interviewAnswer: 2D convolutions model height and width, while 3D convolutions also model depth and can learn cross-slice volumetric context directly. The trade-off is dramatically higher memory and compute.
why: This comes up whenever your data has volumetric or temporal structure and is especially relevant to medical/scientific imaging.
intuition: A 2D kernel sees local height×width neighborhoods. A 3D kernel also moves through depth, so it can learn relationships between neighboring slices instead of treating them independently.
deepDive: 3D convolutions preserve volumetric context but activation memory grows quickly with depth and spatial resolution. For very large 3D volumes, common compromises are patches, anisotropic kernels, 2.5D multi-view models or hybrid architectures.
code:
import torch.nn as nn
conv2d = nn.Conv2d(1, 32, kernel_size=3, padding=1)
conv3d = nn.Conv3d(1, 32, kernel_size=3, padding=1)
commonMistakes: Saying a 3D CNN “directly creates 3D images” regardless of task—the architecture still needs a suitable input/output design.
followUps: How would you train on 1024³ volumes?
Why could plane-wise processing create inconsistency?
production: Benchmark memory, throughput and accuracy. Patch extraction, overlap/blending and distributed inference may be required for large volumes.
workedExample: For CT, MRI or materials volumes, a 3D-aware model can improve cross-slice consistency but may require patch-based training because full-volume activations exceed practical GPU memory.

visual.title: 2D vs 3D convolution
visual.caption: The right choice depends on whether the third dimension carries meaningful local structure and whether compute allows volumetric processing.
